items.title: A precise balance can give entirely wrong masses
items.claim: An electronic balance might read to 0.0001 g — extremely precise. If it has not been calibrated, it might report 5.0732 g when the true mass is 5.0000 g. Precision is not accuracy.
items.prompt: What is the difference between precision and accuracy?

options.text: Precision means repeated measurements agree closely with each other (low random error). Accuracy means measurements agree with the true value (low systematic error). A precise instrument can still be systematically wrong
Precision is about decimal places only
Accuracy depends on temperature, precision does not

items.reveal:
Calibrating a balance with a certified reference mass (e.g. a 5.0000 g class-1 standard) tells you how much to add or subtract from every reading.

Calibrate a pH meter with two buffer standards (typically pH 4.00 and 7.00) before use. Calibrate a thermometer at the ice point (0°C) and boiling point (100°C at 1 atm).

All quantitative chemistry depends on this. An uncalibrated burette, balance or pH meter can give numbers that match each other (precise) and are all wrong (inaccurate). Modern analytical labs include certified reference materials in every batch to catch drift.
items.why: Students conflate precision (consistency) with accuracy (truth). Both matter, and an instrument can be one without the other.

items.title: Metals conduct heat AND electricity well because the same particles carry both
items.claim: Diamond is one of the best heat conductors known but doesn't conduct electricity. Copper is excellent at both. Wood is poor at both. The Wiedemann-Franz law links thermal and electrical conductivity of metals to a universal ratio.
items.prompt: Why is the ratio of thermal to electrical conductivity nearly constant across metals?

options.text: Free electrons in a metal carry both heat and charge; the ratio of thermal to electrical conductivity equals (pi squared over 3) times (k_B over e) squared times T — the Lorenz number — independent of which metal
Metals contain hidden phonons that scale with electrical conductivity

items.reveal_title: One sea of electrons does two jobs
items.reveal:
Metals have a sea of delocalised electrons free to move under an applied voltage (giving electrical conductivity) or under a temperature gradient (giving thermal conductivity).

The Wiedemann-Franz law (1853) predicts the ratio kappa/sigma = L * T, where L is the Lorenz number (about 2.44 x 10 to the minus 8 W ohm per K squared). Most metals at room temperature agree with this to within 10 percent.

Diamond breaks the pattern: it conducts heat via lattice vibrations (phonons) but has no free electrons. Wood is poor at both because it has neither significant free electrons nor an efficient phonon network.
items.why: Heat and electricity look like separate phenomena. In metals, the same charge carriers do both jobs — quantitatively.

items.title: Gold is yellow because its electrons move at over half the speed of light
items.claim: Silver, copper and gold all sit in Group 11. Silver is shiny white, copper reddish, gold yellow. Gold's colour is a direct consequence of special relativity acting on its inner electrons.

options.text: Gold's 1s electrons move at about 58 percent the speed of light; relativistic mass increase contracts the 6s orbital and shrinks the 5d-to-6s gap into the visible — blue is absorbed, yellow is reflected
Gold's surface oxidises to a yellow film
Gold absorbs longer wavelengths because it is denser

items.reveal:
For silver (Z=47) the analogous d-to-s transitions sit in the ultraviolet; silver reflects all visible light evenly. For gold (Z=79) the energy gap collapses into the visible blue and absorbs around 470 nm. The complementary colour — yellow — is what bounces back at your eye.

The same relativistic 6s contraction weakens metallic bonding in mercury (Z=80), giving it a melting point of -39°C and making it the only metal liquid at room temperature.

Without special relativity, gold would be silvery white and mercury would be a solid metal like cadmium above it.
items.why: Colour is treated as an unchanging elemental property. For heavy elements it depends on relativistic effects on inner electrons.
